title: Vibe Coding Examples: 10 Apps to Build First
summary: Real vibe coding examples: what people build, the first prompt for each, and the part that breaks after the demo works.
body_markdown:
*Ten examples of what people build with vibe coding: each one carries the prompt that starts the build and the upkeep the app needs once it works.*


Most vibe coding examples fit a short list: personal trackers, admin panels, dashboards, client portals, booking pages, one-page sites. The list is worth knowing before you start, because the examples people still use months later share one pattern: the app does a single job, on data someone already has, and one person owns it.


The term came from Andrej Karpathy. On February 2, 2025 he wrote: "There's a new kind of coding I call 'vibe coding', where you fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists." He described building weekend projects by saying what he wanted and accepting what came back: "I just see stuff, say stuff, run stuff, and copy paste stuff, and it mostly works." Both quotes appear in[Ars Technica's writeup of the post](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2025/03/is-vibe-coding-with-ai-gnarly-or-reckless-maybe-some-of-both/) from March 2025, and Karpathy was clear about the limits: the approach suited throwaway work.


If you're new to the term itself, our guide to[what vibe coding is](https://www.vybe.build/blog/what-is-vibe-coding) covers the definition and how it differs from regular AI-assisted coding.


Below are ten examples. Each has the prompt that gets a first version out and the part that usually breaks once the demo works.


## What people build with vibe coding


Two kinds of builds dominate the examples in the wild: personal tools and work tools. The personal ones (carb counters, mood journals, story generators, small games) make good first projects because a mistake costs an evening. The work tools are where the examples end up running a real process, and those need more care: real data, access rules, an owner.


The habit is mainstream now. In[Stack Overflow's 2025 developer survey](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai) , 84% of respondents said they were using or planning to use AI tools in their development process, up from 76% the year before. The same survey found people divided on the output: 46% said they actively distrust the accuracy of AI tools, against 33% who trust it. Building a first version is quick. Checking it against real data is the slower half of every example below.


## The ten examples at a glance


- An expense tracker you keep using.
- An admin panel for a small team.
- A client portal.
- A custom CRM for a tiny sales team.
- An approval workflow.
- An inventory counter.
- A booking page.
- An internal FAQ with search.
- A form that replaces a spreadsheet.
- A weekly report generator.


## 10 vibe coding examples


Ordered from the ones you can start tonight to the ones that need a little planning.


### 1. An expense tracker you keep using


You open one page, type what you spent, pick a category and see the month's totals. It works because the data is yours and the job is small.


Start with this prompt: "Build a simple expense tracker: a form with amount, category and date, a list of this month's entries, and totals by category. Store the entries so they survive a refresh."


After the first version comes exporting, recurring entries and fixing mistakes. The break shows up a week in: the totals look right, then you find the same lunch logged twice, because nothing checks for duplicates.


### 2. An admin panel for a small team


This build gives you one screen with the numbers that matter today, a table you can filter and a status you can change from the row.


Start with this prompt: "Build an admin dashboard with a summary row, a table of recent orders I can filter by status, and the ability to change a status from the table."


The first version works on the twenty rows you typed in yourself. The first real import of thousands of rows is where it gets slow or quietly wrong. Plan that import before you celebrate the panel.


### 3. A client portal


Clients log in and see their own files, status and invoices instead of emailing you for updates. (This is the kind of app we see teams build in Vybe all the time, for what it's worth.)


Start with this prompt: "Build a client portal: each client sees only their own projects, files and current status, with a simple login."


Test access control first, before you invite anyone. The common failure is a link that isn't scoped to one client, or a status page that shows a project it shouldn't. Check with two accounts before the first real user arrives.


### 4. A custom CRM for a tiny sales team


This one holds contacts, a pipeline with stages and notes on each deal, and two people can run it without a setup project.


Start with this prompt: "Build a simple CRM: a contacts list, a deal pipeline with four stages I can drag between, and notes on each contact."


The pipeline looks done on day one. The pain shows up later, when two people edit the same deal and one change quietly overwrites the other. If the team is more than one person, decide early who wins a conflict.


### 5. An approval workflow


You submit a request form, a manager approves or rejects, and everyone can see where a request sits.


Start with this prompt: "Build a time-off request flow: employees submit a request with dates, a manager sees pending requests and approves or rejects, and the requester gets the decision."


It works for one approver. It stops working the day the manager is on leave, if the app never says who steps in. Define the fallback before the first real request arrives.


### 6. An inventory counter


You track items with quantities, count stock down and get a warning when something drops below its minimum.


Start with this prompt: "Build an inventory tracker for a small bakery: items with quantities, buttons to count stock down, and a warning when anything drops below its minimum."


Two people counting at once is the failure mode: the second count erases the first, and the warning never fires. A counter needs a record of who counted and when, which is the prompt people forget.


### 7. A booking page


The page shows available slots for the next two weeks, takes a form, sends a confirmation and marks the slot as taken.


Start with this prompt: "Build a booking page for a barber: show available slots for the next two weeks, let a client pick one and leave their name, and mark the slot as taken."


Double-booking is the classic break: two people click the same slot in the same minute and both get a confirmation. The fix is a lock on the slot, one more prompt away.


### 8. An internal FAQ with search


The team gets questions and answers with a search box that filters as you type, and anyone can edit an entry.


Start with this prompt: "Build an internal FAQ: a list of questions with answers, a search box that filters as I type, and an edit button for each entry."


Answers go stale after a few months, people stop trusting them, and the FAQ becomes one more tab people skip. Give each answer an owner and a review date.


### 9. A form that replaces a spreadsheet


You get structured fields, validation on every field and a sortable table of submissions.


Start with this prompt: "Build an onboarding form for new hires: fields for name, start date, equipment and manager, validation on every field, and a table of all submissions I can sort."


The form collects data cleanly. Then it sits in its own table while the real work stays in the old spreadsheet, because the process never switched over. The switch is part of the project: pick a date, retire the sheet, run both in parallel until then. We wrote a full guide on[replacing spreadsheets with custom apps](https://www.vybe.build/blog/replace-spreadsheets-with-custom-apps) .


### 10. A weekly report generator


Every Monday, the report shows the week's new records grouped by status, with a line on what changed since last week.


Start with this prompt: "Build a weekly report: every Monday show the week's new records grouped by status, with a one-line summary of what changed since last week."


The report renders on day one with whatever demo data the prototype was seeded with. Wiring it to your real data is the actual project, and it's the part a demo never shows. Start the wiring before you share the first report.


## What the examples that last have in common


Four things show up in the builds that survive their first month. The app does one job, and only that job. The data was real from day one, or someone committed to making it real. One person owns it: they answer questions, fix drift and retire it when it stops earning its keep. And someone checks the output against reality, because the model writes confident code that can still be wrong. A tracker that under-counts is worse than a missing tracker: you trust the number and order the wrong amount.


## How to pick your first example


Match the project to what you already have. If your data lives in a spreadsheet, start with the form and the table. If your week is full of handoffs and chasing, start with the approval workflow. If people keep asking you the same questions, start with the internal FAQ. If clients email you for status, start with the portal. If it were my first build, I would start with the form: lowest stakes, clearest job.


For the prompts, our[vibe coding prompts guide](https://www.vybe.build/blog/vibe-coding-prompts) has 30 ready-made templates plus a fill-in structure for writing your own. For the method end to end, read[how to vibe code](https://www.vybe.build/blog/how-to-vibe-code) . For the failure patterns,[the mistakes people make while vibe coding](https://www.vybe.build/blog/vibe-coding-mistakes) covers most of them. And if the app will touch customer data, read[whether vibe coding is safe](https://www.vybe.build/blog/is-vibe-coding-safe) before you put anything real in it.


## FAQ


### What are some examples of vibe coding?


Small, single-job apps are the common cases: expense trackers, admin panels, client portals, small CRMs, approval flows, inventory counters, booking pages, internal FAQs, spreadsheet replacements and report generators. Personal projects like trackers and small games are the other big group. The ten examples above cover both.


### What is a good first vibe coding project?


Pick something with data you already have and low stakes. A personal tracker or a form that replaces one spreadsheet are the usual starting points: the job is clear, the data is yours, and a mistake costs little. Save the client portal and anything touching customer data for later.


### Can you vibe code a real business app?


Yes, and plenty of teams do. The difference from a weekend build is what comes after the first version: access control, wiring to real data, an owner and a checking habit. Without those four, it stays a demo.
